job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Elena Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents in Kingsley and I treat the job hunt like a job. I'm up at seven, I run for half an hour, and from nine to one I apply, practise security challenges online and write to people on a professional network. Afternoons I study for a security certificate, and in the evening I walk the dog with my dad. I use an AI assistant for nearly everything, from debugging to rehearsing interview answers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you. What was your degree and what did you do for your internship?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Computer science, with cybersecurity modules, at Hartley University. My final project was a tool that flags phishing emails by their writing style, and it caught eight out of ten in my test set, which I was pleased with. My internship was ten weeks on the IT help desk at a regional bank, resetting passwords and watching how a real security team works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I expected, and it means my skills are still worth what they were. I'd tell friends that the hype was always bigger than the product, though the products are useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately my situation doesn't change. There are plenty of security and IT jobs near Kingsley, but there are also many graduates, and entry roles want a certificate I don't have yet. My savings and my parents mean I can wait about a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my routine, finish the security certificate by February, and apply to the bank's graduate programme again. I'd also join a local security meet-up, since a lot of hiring happens by conversation. And I'd keep using AI for coding and practice, since it saves hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a good outcome for someone like me, and my money's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the graduate programme again. What happened the first time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I got to the final round and then got a polite no. They said I was strong technically but they'd chosen someone with more customer-facing experience. I've been working on that since.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you work on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I volunteer at a charity's computer club, helping older people spot scam messages. It's good practice at explaining things simply.

I'd tell friends the hype was bigger than the product.
think: My situation doesn't change: many graduates chase **entry roles** that want a certificate I lack.
Savings and my parents let me wait about a **year**.
do: Apply to the bank's **graduate programme** again.
Join a local **security meet-up**, since hiring often happens by conversation.
feel: **Calm**: it's a good outcome for someone like me, and money's fine.
S0.quote: The hype was always bigger than the product, though the products are useful.
fieldNote: Secure and **methodical**, and she treats the search as a structured job.
Reached a final round before and learned the gap was **customer-facing** experience.
**Volunteers** at a charity computer club to build that skill.

steps.text: Finish the security certificate by February

Go to a local security meet-up each month
Keep volunteering at the charity computer club

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift, but it's one with openings. I'd tell friends that people who learn to work with these tools will do better, and I'd tell older relatives not to be scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think routine security work, like scanning logs, writing reports and triaging alerts, is the first to be automated. So entry roles shrink, but there's more demand for people who understand what the tools miss. I'm fairly well placed, but the first rung is harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd specialise now, in something AI-related like checking and defending AI systems. I'd build a portfolio with two public projects and apply to firms that build or use security tools. I'd also ask the bank's security lead, Mr Hall, for a conversation about where the team's heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I think I'll be okay, but I'm aware many friends won't have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who work with the tools do better. What if they don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be wrong about the whole bet, and I'd have to move into something more physical, like running secure hardware or data centres. I keep that as a backup in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who among your friends worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana, who did a general computing degree and doesn't specialise in anything. She applies to every post and gets nowhere. I'd tell my friend to pick one niche, even if it feels like closing doors.

I'd tell older relatives not to be scared.

fieldNote: Bets on specialising, with a **physical-hardware** plan B in her head.

Seeks inside **information** from her internship contacts.

steps.text: Build two public projects on defending AI systems

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have two years to build some safety nets, and that governments should think about income support and retraining immediately. I'd post about it and I'd probably join a campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately that one scares me. Security work is thinking work, so a machine does most of it by 2028, and entry-level posts would be among the first gone. I'm better than most at using the tools, but if the tools do the work, that edge shrinks too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any decent security or IT job within six months, even if it's not my dream. I'd move my savings to something safer and cut back on anything extra. I'd also look at physical security and critical infrastructure work, which lasts a few years longer than screen work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit thrown. I can act, but I don't see one clean way through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your edge shrinks if the tools do the work. What's left of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Judgement, I hope, and trust. A bank won't hand its security to something no human has signed off on. But I'm not certain that holds for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum says look after yourself and not to panic. Dad says learn a trade. I think both of them are right, which is annoying.

say: We have two years to build **safety nets**, starting with income support and retraining.
I'd post about it and join a **campaign**.
think: Security work is thinking work, so a machine does most of it by **2028** and entry posts go first.
My tool skills help, but that edge **shrinks** too.
do: Take any decent security or IT **job** within six months.
Move my savings somewhere **safer** and cut extras.
Look into **physical security** and critical infrastructure work.
feel: **Anxious** and a bit thrown: I can act, but see no clean way through.
S2.quote: A bank won't hand its security to something no human has signed off on.
fieldNote: **Anxious** rather than alarmed because her skills and family cushion give her moves.
Hopes human **judgement** and sign-off keep value.
Gets **different** advice from each parent and finds both fair.

steps.text: Take any decent security or IT job within six months
Move savings into a safer account and cut extras
Apply for physical security and infrastructure roles
Join a campaign for retraining and income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years I'd say is enough to prepare but not enough to relax. I'd say that universities, employers and governments should start talking now, and I'd tell friends to specialise early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's probably okay. I could get a job, build experience in a year or two and move toward oversight work, checking what the AI systems do. By 2031 I'd have a name in a small area. The worry is the people who haven't started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the best offer in the next six months, then keep studying toward advanced certificates. I'd put away a third of my pay. And I'd probably start a master's part-time in year three if the market's rough, because that's the sort of time to be learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steady. I like having years to work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a master's in year three, not now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd rather earn and see a real workplace. Later, if the entry roles have thinned out, being in a course with some funding is a better place to be than competing for jobs that don't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger cousin starting an IT degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get one good summer internship, learn to explain your work to non-experts, and don't bet everything on a single skill.

I'd tell friends to specialise **early**, while there's still time to choose.
think: For me it's probably **okay**: a job, experience, then oversight work checking AI systems.
I worry about people who haven't **started**.
do: Take the best **offer** within six months.

fieldNote: Sees time as room to build a niche in AI **oversight**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough to do a lot, and I'd say to everyone, make a plan and write it down. I'd also push my local council to fund adult courses, because the time is only useful if people can use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's close to good news. I'd have a decade to become senior, maybe lead a team that audits AI systems. By 2036 the work will look different, but that's normal for a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job, get certified, move up and keep a rainy-day fund. I'd mentor graduates after a few years, since I know how hard the start is. And I'd write a blog about security for ordinary people, which builds a name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the version where I can say I'm lucky and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first year be, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A job in a security operations team, a six-month review with my manager, and a fixed amount into savings. I'd also keep running the computer club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry about being too comfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Comfortable people get surprised, so I'd check my plan once a year, and read about it every month.

say: Ten years is long enough to do a lot, so everyone should **write a plan**.
I'd push the council to fund **adult courses**.
think: For me it's close to **good news**: a decade to become senior or lead an audit team.
The work will look different by 2036, which is **normal** for a career.
do: Take a **first job** in security operations and get certified.
Keep a **rainy-day fund** and mentor graduates later.
Write a **blog** about security for ordinary people.
feel: **Calm**: this is the version where I can say I'm lucky and mean it.
S4.quote: Comfortable people get surprised, so I'd check my plan once a year
fieldNote: Calm but **self-aware**, and she builds a yearly plan check into her future.
Sees **community** work as part of her career.

steps.text: Join a security operations team and get certified

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one is the one that makes me stop and think, because I can't see a clean way through it. I'd still be fine compared to many. What would help is practical: free retraining, honest news from employers and somewhere to talk it through.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume my generation is either doomed or lucky. Mostly I'm just trying to work out the next step, with tools my parents never had and a market they don't recognise.

headlineQuote: People assume my generation is either doomed or lucky. Mostly I'm just trying to work out the next step, with tools my parents never had
portrait: Elena is a **23-year-old** computer science graduate with a cybersecurity focus, living with her parents and still waiting on a first offer.
She is a **pragmatic centrist** who judges change by what it does, and her bank help-desk internship shaped her view of risk.
She uses **AI tools** daily and treats the job hunt like a job, so she acts early and keeps adjusting her plan.
Her mood is **calm** when little changes, uneasy in Steady Disruption and anxious in the 2028 world.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, since she can't see a clean route through it even with her skills.
whatWouldHelp: Free **retraining**, honest news from employers and **someone to talk** it through with.
